accepted.match: "irony" defined differently in tone and irony
accepted.reason: Compatible depth difference: tone gives a one-line gloss of irony as a gap between wording and meaning, while the irony lesson defines the full three-type literary figure. They do not contradict; the tone lesson explicitly treats irony as a complicating factor for tone claims.

accepted.match: "context" defined differently in symbolism and irony
accepted.reason: Compatible definitions at different scopes: symbolism defines context generally (surrounding text, genre, culture, history shaping meaning); irony applies that same notion to the specific job of recognizing an ironic gap. No contradiction.

accepted.match: "repetition" defined differently in symbolism and rhetorical-analysis
accepted.reason: Genuine homonym across sub-disciplines: symbolism uses repetition as the reappearance of a detail that accumulates significance; rhetorical-analysis uses repetition as a deliberate word/phrase strategy for emphasis. Both are correct in their owning lessons.

accepted.match: "mixed metaphor" defined differently in metaphor and simile
accepted.reason: Compatible: both define it as combining inconsistent or incongruous comparison images in one construction. The wording differs but the concept agrees.

accepted.match: "simile" defined differently in metaphor and simile
accepted.reason: Compatible depth difference: metaphor's lesson gives a brief cross-reference definition ('explicit comparison with like/as, covered in its own lesson'), while the simile lesson owns the full definition. Consistent with each other.

accepted.match: "summary" defined differently in fiction and writing-about-literature
accepted.reason: Genuine homonym: fiction defines summary as a narrative mode (compressing narrated time), while writing-about-literature defines summary as condensing a source's ideas in one's own words. Different senses, both correct in context.

accepted.match: "counterargument" defined differently in rhetorical-analysis and argument
accepted.reason: Compatible: rhetorical-analysis frames counterargument as a persuasion strategy (acknowledging opposing views), argument frames it as the opposing position itself to be addressed fairly. Same concept, complementary emphasis; no contradiction.
